# Andhakaraṇa Sutta (Iti 87 (It 3.38 PTS It 82))

**ID:** Iti 87 (It 3.38 PTS It 82)
**Section:** Itivuttaka (iti)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Andhakaraṇa Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0504m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Andhakaraṇa Sutta* ("Destroyers of Sight", Iti 87; PTS It 82) is a discourse found in the *Itivuttaka* concerning mental cultivation and discernment [Windisch 1889]. In this sutta, the Buddha contrasts three types of unskillful thinking (*akusalavitakkā*) with three types of skillful thinking (*kusalavitakkā*) [Windisch 1889]. The three unskillful thoughts—sensual thinking (*kāmavitakka*), ill-will thinking (*vyāpādavitakka*), and cruel or harmful thinking (*vihiṃsāvitakka*)—are described by a stock formula as sight-destroying (*andhakaraṇa*), causing lack of vision (*acakkhukaraṇa*), producing ignorance (*aññāṇakaraṇa*), obstructing wisdom (*paññānirodhika*), conducive to vexation (*vighātapakkhika*), and not leading to Nibbāna (*anibbānasamvattanika*) [Windisch 1889]. Conversely, their opposites—beginning with thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*)—are sight-producers (*cakkhukaraṇa*), promote knowledge and wisdom, and lead directly to Nibbāna [Windisch 1889].
